pull.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pull.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

On the approach: first 4 commits look great and straightforwardly improve error handling. Initial concern i had earlier about trying to predict whether paths were writable is resolved and well handled. 

The last commit should also be a net improvement, but is more of a mixed bag. The last commit provides a potentially significant benefit because it delays deleting the original wallet database until the new sqlite database is fully created, so if there are errors creating it, the old wallet will be left in place, and it it can be migrated again later (or dumped or opened in an old version of bitcoin core) without the user manually needing to restore from the backup file.

The downside of the last commit is it adds more complexity to code that is already pretty complex, and leaves filesystem in a slightly messier state because if creating and populating the sqlite database fails there will now be two copies of the original bdb database instead of one.

More ideally the code would get rid of all these deletes and renames and backups and restores and just leave the original data exactly where it is during the migration, writing the new data to temporary directory. Then do simple renames if the migration succeeds, renaming the old wallet to have a migrated_<timestamp> suffix and renaming the new wallet directories in its place.

This is possibly orthogonal, but I just had the thought that maybe we can achieve some additional robustness in migration by first migrating to an in-memory sqlite database, and then only writing that out to disk when migration is successful. wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures

Currently, MigrateToSQLite loads all BDB records into memory,
deletes the original database, creates the sqlite db in its
place, and writes the records to it. If anything fails after the
delete, the wallet is left partly in sqlite format with legacy
records, and the user has to restore the backup manually.

Instead, build the sqlite db in a temporary directory next to the
original db file, and once all records are written, rename it into
place. For wallet directories, the rename atomically replaces the
original wallet.dat, so any earlier failure leaves the original
untouched. A plain file wallet becomes a wallet directory, which
can't replace the file atomically, so the original file is erased
just before the move.

Before the move, check that no other files of the db, such as a
leftover journal, are at the destination, and fail if one is.
SQLite would otherwise roll a leftover journal back into the new
db when opening it, corrupting it.

Failures once the original db may have been erased or replaced
throw, so the migration restores the backup.

Code review ACK 399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd. This is a clear improvement over master, which deletes the original database before writing the new one and asserts if anything fails after that. Now the new database is fully built before it replaces the original, failures after that point restore the backup, and a leftover journal at the wallet location stops the migration instead of corrupting the new database.

Thanks for taking the last suggestions. Since my last review the only changes besides the rebase move into migration.cpp are the ones from that review.

Possible follow-ups after merging:

1. **Failures in `MoveDatabase` before the rename delete and restore the untouched original.** For a wallet directory, an error like the leftover file check happens before anything is replaced, but `MigrateToSQLite` [throws](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd/src/wallet/migration.cpp#L173-L176), so the rollback deletes the original `wallet.dat` and copies the backup back. If that copy fails, the user has to restore the backup by hand. `MoveDatabase` could report whether it replaced the destination, so this can return false instead ([patch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4681646376), also raised by [w0xlt](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#pullrequestreview-5935190787) and the [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd-3083-8.html#finding-finding%3A2)).
2. **A stray `return false` after the point of no return would skip the restore.** Returning an enum from `MigrateToSQLite`, or a result that says whether the original was touched, would make this contract part of the type instead of a comment. It fits together with item 1 ([comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4589667952)).
3. **The error doesn't say when the backup was restored.** After a failed migration whose restore succeeds, the user only sees the failure message, so they can't tell whether they still need to restore the `.legacy.bak` themselves. This is also the case on master for `DoMigration` failures ([comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4682560565)).
4. **A new watch-only or solvables wallet can be left behind.** If [`CWallet::CreateNew`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd/src/wallet/migration.cpp#L467-L471) fails or throws after `MakeWalletDatabase` created its database, `out_wallet` stays empty, so the rollback doesn't remove the new `<name>_watchonly` or `<name>_solvables` wallet, and a retry would likely fail because that wallet already exists. This predates the PR.
5. **A temporary database can be left in the wallet directory.** If [`RunWithinTxn`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd/src/wallet/migration.cpp#L148) throws (SQLite statement setup in `MakeBatch` can), it skips [`remove_tmp_and_fail`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd/src/wallet/migration.cpp#L129-L141), and the rollback needlessly restores the untouched original as in item 1. The same leftover happens if the node is killed during migration. The `_sqlite_<time>.tmp` directory then holds a valid SQLite wallet that `listwalletdir` lists, and later migrations use a new name, so they don't remove it ([Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd-3083-8.html#finding-finding%3A4)).
6. **A concurrent `loadwallet` could open the database between the rename and the reopen.** Migration doesn't reserve the wallet name the way `LoadWallet` does, so a `loadwallet` for the same name in that window could lock the moved database and make the reopen fail. This needs an unlikely concurrent call ([comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4551983828), from the [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-8a9c3af0eb7df50f38ca511491d3d0d1e47f7fb7-2505-5.html#finding-finding%3A2)).
7. **The temporary path isn't reserved.** The [existence check](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd/src/wallet/migration.cpp#L111-L114) and `MakeDatabase` are separate steps, so if something else creates that path in between, `remove_tmp_and_fail` would delete its contents. Creating the directory with `fs::create_directory` and continuing only if this call created it would close the gap ([Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd-3083-8.html#finding-finding%3A3)).
8. **Some failure paths have no tests:** transaction begin, write and commit failures in `MigrateToSQLite`, and a descriptor import failing in the watch-only or solvables wallet. Covering them needs a way to inject failures ([transaction failures](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd-3083-8.html#finding-finding%3A5), [descriptor import](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd-3083-8.html#finding-finding%3A6)).
9. **The catch doesn't reset `success`.** If something throws after [`success = DoMigration(...)`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd/src/wallet/migration.cpp#L622-L634) is set (as far as I can see only an allocation failure in `GetAllScriptPubKeyMans()`), migration continues as if it succeeded, with `error` set. Setting `success = false` in the catch would send every exception through the restore path. Low priority, since the migration itself has completed in that case ([Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-59110addfd4d767b86b64e112c4e7e5cd88598f3-3011-7.html#finding-finding%3A6)).
10. **Longer term, the original wallet could stay untouched for the whole migration**, with everything new written to a temporary location and renamed into place at the end, which would remove the point of no return entirely ([discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#pullrequestreview-4566894731), [achow101's in-memory variant](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#issuecomment-6666823474)).

More generally, `MigrateLegacyToDescriptor` treats a false return from `MigrateToSQLite` as "the original is untouched" and skips the restore, while an exception gets the full rollback. That makes it easy for a future change to add a `return false` after the point of no return without noticing ([the comment on the final cleanup](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553133860) is one place where this matters). In commit "test: migrate a wallet with a leftover journal at its location" (59110addfd4d767b86b64e112c4e7e5cd88598f3)

Since `migrate_and_get_rpc` only resets mocktime after `migratewallet` returns, calling it for a migration that is expected to fail leaves the node's mock time set for the tests that follow. It's harmless right now, but calling `migratewallet` directly here after copying the wallet, as `test_db_named_as_journal` does, would avoid it. The [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/report/34193-59110addfd4d767b86b64e112c4e7e5cd88598f3-3011-7.html#finding-finding%3A5) pointed this out.

In commit "wallet: migration, restore backup if an exception is thrown" (2302ba1c6e2a44903301a787a2cf37865fba8d90)

Would suggest changing "Unexpected exception during migration" to "Migration failed". Unexpected exception sounds like an internal bug, but most of what lands here are just runtime failures: the `MoveDatabase` errors rethrown in `MigrateToSQLite` (including the leftover file error, which tells the user how to fix it), filesystem errors like a full disk or missing permissions, and SQLite errors.

Separately, and probably for a follow-up since it applies to `DoMigration` failures on master too: when the restore below succeeds, the error doesn't say that the original wallet was restored, so the user can't tell whether they need to restore the backup themselves.

re: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4686308536

> just in case we ever change the process to clean stale journals automatically

Makes sense to keep the test as a guard, thanks.

On the cleanup idea itself, I'd don't think it makes sense to silently a delete a file if don't know how it got there. Better to prompt the user in this case. If there is actually a known scenario that could leave these files behind, it could make sense to try to handle that case automatically, but even then I think a good way to handle it would probably be to warn the user and rename the files, not silently delete them.
